rows: Identify fiber, yarn size, twist, sett, weave structure, beat, and finishing.
The same yarn can produce stiff or drapey cloth depending on sett and interlacement.
Start with WPI, then adjust for plain weave, twill, warp-faced, weft-faced, or lace structures.
WPI rules of thumb are sampling starts, not guarantees.
Match shaft count, shed quality, width, tension needs, portability, and pattern complexity.
A simple loom can make complex cloth slowly; a complex loom mainly expands control and repeatability.
Check float length, interlacement frequency, abrasion risk, drape, and shaft requirements.
Longer floats improve sheen/drape but reduce snag resistance.
Decide whether image/detail comes from weft dominance, warp dominance, pickup, or color order.
Tapestry is structure plus design process, not just a heavy wall fabric.
Look for uneven tension, wrong sett, skipped threads, draw-in, beat inconsistency, and finishing shrinkage.
Many "weave structure" problems are actually tension or finishing problems.
